label: conj-GGL
title: Conjecture
body_md:
\label{conj-GGL}
Let $X$ be a smooth projective variety and $D$ a simple normal crossings divisor such that $K_X + D$ is big. Then there is some proper subvariety $S \subsetneq X$ containing the images of all nonconstant holomorphic maps $\mathbb{C} \to X \setminus D$, i.e. $X\setminus D$ is pseudo Brody hyperbolic.
head: environment

label: conj-algGGL
title: Conjecture
body_md:
\label{conj-algGGL}
Let $X$ be a smooth projective variety and $D$ be a simple normal crossings divisor such that $K_X + D$ is big. Then there exists an $\epsilon > 0$ and a subvariety $S \subsetneq X$ such that every map $f: C\to X$ from a smooth projective curve $C$ that is birational onto its image and $f(C)\not\subset D\cup S$ satisfies
$$ 2g(C) - 2 + |f^{-1}(D)| > \epsilon \deg f^* L$$
where $L$ is an ample line bundle on $X$ and $g(C)$ is the geometric genus of $C$.

label: prop-mainSetupProp
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop-mainSetupProp}
Suppose that for a very general hypersurface $D$ of degree $d$ in ${{\mathbb P}}^n$ there exists a smooth curve $Y$ of genus $g$ mapping birationally to ${{\mathbb P}}^n$ with image of degree $e$ and meeting $D$ precisely $i$ times. Then there exists an \'{e}tale map $B \to H^0({\mathcal O}_{{{\mathbb P}}^n}(d))$ and a $GL(n+1)$-invariant family ${\mathcal Y}$ over $B$ such that a general fiber $Y_b$ of $\mathcal{Y} \to B$ is a smooth genus $g$ curve mapping birationally to ${{\mathbb P}}^n$ with degree $e$ and meeting $D_b$ precisely $i$ times. Furthermore, for a general $b \in B$ there is an exact sequence of sheaves
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=small]
0 \ar{r} & T_{{\mathcal Y}}^{\operatorname{vert}}(-\log {\mathcal D})|_{Y_b} \ar{r} & f^*T_{{\mathcal X}}^{\operatorname{vert}}(- \log {\mathcal D})|_{Y_b} \ar{r} & N_{Y_b/{{\mathbb P}}^n}(\log D_b) \ar{r} & 0.
\end{tikzcd} 
\]
head: environment

label: prop-2.2
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop-2.2}
	The quotient $\left(f^*T_{\mathcal X}^{\operatorname{vert}}(-\log {\mathcal D})\right)\big/\left(T_{\mathcal Y}^{\operatorname{vert}}(-\log {\mathcal D})\right)$ of vertical log tangent sheaves is isomorphic to $N_{{\mathcal Y}/{\mathcal X}}(\log {\mathcal D})$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The short exact sequences  (\ref{eqn-lognormalfam}), (\ref{eqn-verticalx}) and (\ref{eqn-verticaly}) fit together in the following commutative diagram, where ${\mathcal K}_1$ denotes the cokernel of the natural inclusion $T_{\mathcal Y}^{\operatorname{vert}}(-\log {\mathcal D}) \hookrightarrow f^*T_{\mathcal X}^{\operatorname{vert}}(-\log {\mathcal D})$:
	\begin{equation*}
		\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=16pt]
		& &0 &0 \\
		& &f^*p_1^*T_{{{\mathbb P}}^n} \arrow[u] \arrow[r,equal] &f^*p_1^*T_{{{\mathbb P}}^n} \arrow[u] \\
		&0 \arrow[r] &T_{\mathcal Y}(-\log {\mathcal D}) \arrow[u] \arrow[r] &f^*T_{\mathcal X}(-\log {\mathcal D}) \arrow[u] \arrow[r] &N_{{\mathcal Y}/{\mathcal X}}(\log {\mathcal D}) \arrow[r] &0\\
		&0 \arrow[r] &T_{\mathcal Y}^{\operatorname{vert}}(-\log {\mathcal D}) \arrow[u] \arrow[r] &f^*T_{\mathcal X}^{\operatorname{vert}}(-\log {\mathcal D}) \arrow[u] \arrow[r] &{\mathcal K}_1 \arrow[r] \arrow[u, "\simeq"] &0\\		
		& &0 \arrow[u] &0 \arrow[u] & &
		\end{tikzcd}
	\end{equation*}
	The required isomorphism follows from the Nine Lemma.
head: environment

label: prop-pullback
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop-pullback}
	For a generic $b\in B$, we have the isomorphism 
	$$\iota_b^*N_{{\mathcal Y}/{\mathcal X}}(\log {\mathcal D})\simeq N_{Y_b/{{\mathbb P}}^n}(\log D_b),$$ 
	where $\iota_b:Y_b\rightarrow {\mathcal Y}$ denotes the inclusion of the fiber.
head: environment

title: Proof
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: We already constructed $B$ and ${\mathcal Y}$ in the discussion at the beginning of this section. It remains to show that the log tangent sheaf $N_{Y_b/{{\mathbb P}}^n}(\log D_b)$ is the cokernel of the map $T_{{\mathcal Y}}^{\operatorname{vert}}|_{Y_b} \to f^* T_{{\mathcal X}}^{\operatorname{vert}}(-\log {\mathcal D})|_{Y_b} $. By Proposition \ref{prop-pullback}, $N_{Y_b/{{\mathbb P}}^n}(\log D_b)$ is the restriction of $N_{{\mathcal Y}/{\mathcal X}}(\log {\mathcal D})$ to $Y_b$. By Proposition \ref{prop-2.2}, we see that $N_{{\mathcal Y}/{\mathcal X}}(\log {\mathcal D})$ is the cokernel of the map of vertical log tangent sheaves. The result follows.

label: prop-mainLazarsfeldProp
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop-mainLazarsfeldProp}
Suppose that for a very general hypersurface $D_b$ of degree $d$ in ${{\mathbb P}}^n$ there exists a smooth curve $Y_b$ of genus $g$ mapping birationally to ${{\mathbb P}}^n$ with image of degree $e$ and $|f^{-1}(D_b)| = i$. Then as in Proposition \ref{prop-mainSetupProp}, there is an exact sequence of sheaves
\[
\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=small]
0 \ar{r} & T_{{\mathcal Y}}^{\operatorname{vert}}(-\log {\mathcal D})|_{Y_b} \ar{r} & f^*T_{{\mathcal X}}^{\operatorname{vert}}(- \log {\mathcal D})|_{Y_b} \ar{r} & N_{Y_b/{{\mathbb P}}^n}(\log D_b) \ar{r} & 0.
\end{tikzcd} 
\]
If $2g-2+i < (d-(2n-1))e$, then $f_b^* p_1^* M_d$ dominates $N_{Y_b/{{\mathbb P}}^n}(\log D_b)$ under the natural inclusion $M_d \to T_{{\mathcal X}}(- \log {\mathcal D})$. Thus, for some general polynomials $P_1, \dots, P_s$, we have a surjection $f_b^*p_1^* M_1^{\oplus s} \to N_{Y_b/{{\mathbb P}}^n}(\log D_b)$.

label: prop-LMinclusion
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop-LMinclusion}
	The pullback $p_1^*M_d$ of the Lazarsfeld bundle naturally injects into the vertical log tangent sheaf $T_{\mathcal X}^{\operatorname{vert}}(-\log {\mathcal D})$, and the cokernel of $p_1^*M_d \hookrightarrow T_{\mathcal X}^{\operatorname{vert}}(-\log {\mathcal D})$ is $p_1^*{\mathcal O}_{{{\mathbb P}}^n}.$

label: diag-1
title: Proof
body_md:
First, we have the following commutative diagram, which contains the short exact sequences (\ref{eqn-logtangent1fam}) and (\ref{eqn-verticalx}). ${\mathcal K}_2$ denotes the cokernel of the natural inclusion $T_{\mathcal X}^{\operatorname{vert}}(-\log {\mathcal D}) \hookrightarrow p_2^*T_B\simeq H^0({\mathcal O}_{{{\mathbb P}}^n}(d))\otimes {\mathcal O}_{\mathcal X}$. The middle column comes from the natural splitting of $T_{\mathcal X}\simeq p_1^*T_{{{\mathbb P}}^n}\oplus p_2^*T_B$.
\begin{equation}\label{diag-1}
	\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=14pt, row sep=12pt]
		& &0 &0 \\
		& &p_1^*T_{{{\mathbb P}}^n} \arrow[u] \arrow[r,equal] &p_1^*T_{{{\mathbb P}}^n} \arrow[u] \\
		&0 \arrow[r] &T_{\mathcal X}(-\log {\mathcal D}) \arrow[u] \arrow[r] &T_{\mathcal X} \arrow[u] \arrow[r] &{\mathcal O}_{\mathcal D}({\mathcal D}) \arrow[r] &0\\
		&0 \arrow[r] &T_{\mathcal X}^{\operatorname{vert}}(-\log {\mathcal D}) \arrow[u] \arrow[r] &p_2^*T_B\simeq H^0({\mathcal O}_{{{\mathbb P}}^n}(d))\otimes {\mathcal O}_{\mathcal X} \arrow[u] \arrow[r] &{\mathcal K}_2 \arrow[r] \arrow[u, "\simeq"] &0\\		
		& &0 \arrow[u] &0 \arrow[u] & &
	\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation}
It follows from the Nine Lemma that ${\mathcal K}_2\simeq {\mathcal O}_{\mathcal D}({\mathcal D})$.

The bottom row of the above diagram induces a natural inclusion $p_1^*M_d \hookrightarrow T_{\mathcal X}^{\operatorname{vert}}(-\log {\mathcal D})$ via the natural restriction map $p_1^*{\mathcal O}_{{{\mathbb P}}^n}(d) \to {\mathcal O}_{\mathcal D}(\mathcal D)$. This gives the following commutative diagram, which contains the bottom row of (\ref{diag-1}) and the pullback of the short exact sequence (\ref{eqn-lm}) via the projection $p:{\mathcal X}\rightarrow {{\mathbb P}}^n$. ${\mathcal K}_3$ denotes the cokernel of $p_1^*M_d \hookrightarrow T_{\mathcal X}^{\operatorname{vert}}(-\log {\mathcal D})$. The right column is obtained by twisting the standard short exact sequence $0 \rightarrow {\mathcal O}_{\mathcal X}(-{\mathcal D}) \rightarrow {\mathcal O}_{\mathcal X} \rightarrow {\mathcal O}_{\mathcal D}\rightarrow 0$
by ${\mathcal O}_{\mathcal X}({\mathcal D})$. Observe that although the first two terms in the right column are both sheaves pulled back from ${{\mathbb P}}^n$, the map between them is not pulled back from ${{\mathbb P}}^n$.
\begin{equation}\label{diag-2}
	\begin{tikzcd}[column sep=13pt, row sep=12pt]
		& & & &0 \arrow[d]\\
		& &0 \arrow[d] & &p_1^*{\mathcal O}_{{{\mathbb P}}^n} \arrow[d]\\
		&0 \arrow[r] &p_1^*M_d \arrow[d] \arrow[r] &H^0({\mathcal O}_{{{\mathbb P}}^n}(d)) \otimes {\mathcal O}_{\mathcal X}\arrow[r] \arrow[d,"="] &p_1^*{\mathcal O}_{{{\mathbb P}}^n}(d) \arrow[r] \arrow[d] &0\\
		&0 \arrow[r] &T_{\mathcal X}^{\operatorname{vert}}(-\log {\mathcal D}) \arrow[d] \arrow[r] &H^0({\mathcal O}_{{{\mathbb P}}^n}(d))\otimes {\mathcal O}_{\mathcal X} \arrow[r] &{\mathcal O}_{{\mathcal D}}({\mathcal D}) \arrow[r] \arrow[d] &0\\
		& &{\mathcal K}_3 \arrow[d] & &0\\
		& &0
	\end{tikzcd}
\end{equation}

It follows from the Snake Lemma that ${\mathcal K}_3\simeq p_1^*{\mathcal O}_{{{\mathbb P}}^n}$.

label: cor-0
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor-0}
	Suppose $d\geq 2n+1$ and $D\subseteq {{\mathbb P}}^n$ is a very general hypersurface of degree $d$. Then $({{\mathbb P}}^n,D)$ is algebraically hyperbolic.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Let the hypersurface be parametrized by $b\in B$, and let $f_b:Y_b\rightarrow X_b={{\mathbb P}}^n$ be a curve of geometric genus $g$ and degree $e$ such that $Y_b\nsubseteq D_b=D$ and $i(Y_b, D)=i$. If $\alpha$ is not generically surjective, then Proposition \ref{prop-notsurj} implies that $$2g-2+i\geq (d-(2n-1))e.$$ If $\alpha$ is generically surjective, then we can apply Proposition \ref{prop-bounds} with $t\leq n-1$. So we obtain $\deg N_{Y_b/{{\mathbb P}}^n}(\log D_b)\geq-(n-1)e,$ and so $2g-2+i\geq (d-2n)e.$

label: lem-2.10
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First consider the case $n\geq 3$. Since rank $N_{Y_b/{{\mathbb P}}^n}(\log D_b)=n-1\geq 2,$ Lemma 2.1 in \cite{Clemens03} implies that $\ker m_1\vert_p$ is independent of the generic polynomial $P_1$ inducing the map $m_1$. Hence, the image of $$\ker m_1\vert_p \xrightarrow{-\otimes H^0({\mathcal O}_{{{\mathbb P}}^n}(d-1))} M_d\vert_p,$$ which is the ideal $H^0({\mathcal O}_{{{\mathbb P}}^n}(d)\otimes I_\ell)$ of some line $\ell=\ell(p,b)$ through $p$, is contained in $\ker \alpha\vert_p$.
    
    For $n=2$, we need a different argument to show that $\ker m_1\vert_p$ is independent of the generic polynomial $P_1$. For this argument, given some $P=P_1\in H^0({\mathcal O}_{{{\mathbb P}}^n}(d-1)),$ we denote the map $m_1$ induced by $P$ as $m_P$, and define $Q_P$ to be the torsion-free part of the image of $m_P$. Since rank $f_b^*p_1^*M_1=2$, $\ker m_P$ and $Q_P$ must have rank one. Now we split into two cases depending on how their degrees compare.
    
    If $\deg \ker m_P\leq \deg Q_P,$ then $\deg Q_P\geq \frac{1}{2}\deg f_b^*p_1^*M_1= -\frac{1}{2}e$, which implies (\ref{eqn-hn}). 
    
    If $\deg \ker m_P> \deg Q_P,$ then $0\subseteq \ker m_P\subseteq f_b^*p_1^*M_1$ is the Harder-Narasimhan filtration, so $\ker m_P$ is independent of $P$, and we can now denote it as $\ker m_1$. The same argument as in the case $n\geq 3$ above implies the existence of some line $\ell=\ell(p,b)$ through $p$ whose ideal $H^0({\mathcal O}_{{{\mathbb P}}^n}(d)\otimes I_\ell)$ is contained in $\ker \alpha\vert_p$.
    
    To prove uniqueness, suppose that there are two distinct lines through $p$ whose ideals are contained in $\ker \alpha\vert_p$. By a dimension count, we would then have $M_d\vert_p=\ker \alpha\vert_p$, which contradicts the assumption that $\alpha_b:f_b^*p_1^*M_d\rightarrow \iota_b^*\alpha$ is generically surjective.
head: environment

label: lem-imRhoDim1
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem-imRhoDim1}
    If $n = 2$, the image of ${\mathcal Y}$ under $\rho$ has dimension at most 1.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $x,y,z$ be the coordinates on ${{\mathbb P}}^2$, and let $p = V(y,z)$, $\ell = V(z)$. Let ${\mathcal Y}_p \subset {\mathcal Y}$ be the fiber over $p_1\circ f: {\mathcal Y} \rightarrow {{\mathbb P}}^2$. Now consider the associated line map $\lambda: {\mathcal Y}_p \dashrightarrow {{\mathbb G}}(1,2)$. Since ${\mathcal Y}$ is $GL(3)$-invariant, $\lambda$ maps onto the locus of lines through $p$. Let ${\mathcal Y}_{p,\ell}$ be the fiber of $\lambda$ over $[\ell]\in {{\mathbb G}}(1,2)$, where $\ell:=\ell(p,b)$. By $GL(3)$-invariance of ${\mathcal Y}$, it is enough to show that ${\mathcal Y}_{p,\ell}$ has one-dimensional image under $\rho$.

    $\rho|_{{\mathcal Y}_{p,\ell}}$ can be decomposed as the composition of $\rho_1: {\mathcal Y}_{p,\ell} \to H^0(\ell,{\mathcal O}_{\ell}(4))$ and $\rho_2: H^0(\ell,{\mathcal O}_{\ell}(4)) \dashrightarrow \overline{U}_{0,4}^{\mathop{\mathrm{Sym}}\nolimits}$. Let $H_{bad} \subset H^0(\ell,{\mathcal O}_{\ell}(4))$ be the locus where $\rho_2$ is not well-defined, namely, the locus of polynomials with at least a triple root union the locus of polynomials with a double root at $p$. If the image of $\rho_1$ is contained in $H_{bad}$, then $\rho$ is not well-defined, so we can assume that the image of $\rho_1$ is not contained in $H_{bad}$.

    By Lemma \ref{lem-2.10}, $H^0({{\mathbb P}}^2,I_{\ell}(4))$ is contained in $T_{\mathcal Y}^{\operatorname{vert}}(-\log {\mathcal D})\vert_{(p,b)}$. Since ${\mathcal Y}_{p,\ell}$ has codimension at most 1 in ${\mathcal Y}_p$, the relative tangent space to $\rho_1$ at $(p,b)$ will consist of a codimension at most 1 space in the affine space \linebreak $F_b + H^0({{\mathbb P}}^2,I_{\ell}(4))$, where $F_b$ is the polynomial defining the quartic plane curve $D_b$. Then, the result follows by a dimension count: the dimension of ${\mathcal Y}_{p,\ell}$ is $\dim {\mathcal Y} - 3 = \dim B - 2$. The dimension of the space of degree 4 polynomials restricting to a particular polynomial on $\ell$ is $\dim H^0({{\mathbb P}}^2,I_{\ell}(4)) = \dim B - 5$, and the dimension of the fibers of $\rho_2: H^0(\ell, {\mathcal O}_{\ell}(4)) \dashrightarrow \overline{U}_{0,4}^{\mathop{\mathrm{Sym}}\nolimits}$ is 3 away from $H_{bad}$. Thus, the dimension of the image of $\rho|_{{\mathcal Y}_{p,\ell}}$ is at most 
    \[ \dim {\mathcal Y}_{p,\ell} - (\dim H^0({{\mathbb P}}^2,I_{\ell}(4)) - 1) - 3 \]
    \[ = \dim B - 2 - (\dim B - 6) - 3 = 1 .\]

label: lem-Ominus2splitting
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem-Ominus2splitting}
For $D$ a general quartic curve, a general line $\ell$ will have $T_{{{\mathbb P}}^2}(-\log D)|_{\ell} \cong {\mathcal O} \oplus {\mathcal O}(-1)$. The space of lines in ${{\mathbb P}}^2$ with $T_{{{\mathbb P}}^2}(- \log D)|_\ell) \cong {\mathcal O}(1) \oplus {\mathcal O}(-2)$ is finite.
head: environment

title: Proof
head: environment

label: lem-P2jumping
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem-P2jumping}
    If the general associated line is not a jumping line for \linebreak $T_{{{\mathbb P}}^2}(-\log D_b)$, then the space $\ker \alpha|_{(p,b)} \subset T_{{\mathcal Y}}^{\operatorname{vert}}(-\log {\mathcal D})|_{(p,b)}$ is generated by $H^0({{\mathbb P}}^2,I_{\ell}(4))$ and $M_1|_p \cdot \operatorname{Jac}(F_b)$. Hence, $T_{{\mathcal Y}}^{\operatorname{vert}}(-\log {\mathcal D})|_{(p,b)}$ is generated by \linebreak $H^0({{\mathbb P}}^2,I_{\ell}(4))$, $M_1|_p\cdot \operatorname{Jac}(F_b)$ and $F_b$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Choose coordinates $x,y,z$ on ${{\mathbb P}}^2$ so that $p = V(y,z)$, $\ell = V(z)$. For convenience, write $F = F_b$. Since we are assuming that $\alpha$ is generically surjective, we work in the case that $\ker \alpha|_{(p,b)}$ has codimension 2 in $T_{{\mathcal X}}^{\operatorname{vert}}(-\log {\mathcal D})|_{(p,b)} = H^0({{\mathbb P}}^2,{\mathcal O}_{{{\mathbb P}}^2}(4))$. 
    We know that $H^0({{\mathbb P}}^2,I_{\ell}(4))$ is contained in $\ker \alpha|_{(p,b)}$, and by $GL(3)$-invariance of ${\mathcal Y}$, it follows that \linebreak $M_1|_p\cdot \operatorname{Jac} (F) = (yF_x, yF_y, yF_z, zF_x, zF_y, zF_z)$ are all contained in $\ker \alpha|_{(p,b)}$. Thus, it remains to show that $\ker \alpha|_{(p,b)}$ is generated by these elements. This will follow if we can show that $H^0({{\mathbb P}}^2,I_{\ell}(4)) + M_1|_p\cdot \operatorname{Jac} (F)$ has codimension 2 in $H^0({{\mathbb P}}^2,{\mathcal O}_{{{\mathbb P}}^2}(4))$.

                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                        
    
    Suppose that $\ell$ is not a jumping line for $T_{{{\mathbb P}}^2}(-\log D_b)$. \cite[Theorem 10]{Marangone} characterizes the non-jumping lines for any vector bundle $\mathcal{E}$ of rank two over ${{\mathbb P}}^2$ as exactly the weak Lefschetz elements for its first cohomology module $H^1_*({{\mathbb P}}^2,\mathcal{E}).$ Let $A={{\mathbb C}}[x,y,z]/Jac(F)$ denote the first cohomology module for $T_{{{\mathbb P}}^2}(-\log D_b)$, and let $A_i$ be the $i$-th graded piece of $A$. Then, it follows that the multiplication map by $z$ is surjective as a map from $A_3 \to A_4$. Thus, we see that $H^0({{\mathbb P}}^2,I_{\ell}(4))$ and $xF_x, xF_y, xF_z, yF_x, yF_y, yF_z$ generate $H^0({{\mathbb P}}^2,{\mathcal O}_{{{\mathbb P}}^2}(4))$. 
     
     We now work modulo $H^0({{\mathbb P}}^2,I_{\ell}(4))$. Since the space $H^0(\ell,{\mathcal O}_{\ell}(4)) = H^0({{\mathbb P}}^2,{\mathcal O}_{{{\mathbb P}}^2}(4)) / H^0({{\mathbb P}}^2,I_{\ell}(4)) $ has dimension 5, the six polynomials $xF_x, xF_y, $ $ xF_z, yF_x, yF_y, yF_z$ must admit a linear relation modulo $H^0({{\mathbb P}}^2,I_{\ell}(4))$. If the relation does not involve the $xF_j$ and only involves $yF_x, yF_y, yF_z$, then it implies a relation among $F_x, F_y, F_z$, and hence, a relation among $xF_x, xF_y, xF_z$. Thus, there must be some relation among $xF_x, xF_y, xF_z, yF_x, yF_y, yF_z$ that involves at least one of $xF_x, xF_y$, and $xF_z$. In particular, it follows that $M_1|_p\cdot \operatorname{Jac} (F)$ has codimension at most 2 in $H^0({{\mathbb P}}^2,{\mathcal O}_{{{\mathbb P}}^2}(4)) / H^0({{\mathbb P}}^2,I_{\ell}(4))$ as required.

     For general $b$, note that $F_b$ does not vanish at $p$, so $F_b$ is not in $\ker \alpha|_{(p,b)}$, but it clearly is in $T_{{\mathcal Y}}^{\operatorname{vert}}(-\log {\mathcal D})|_{(p,b)}$. The result follows.
head: environment

label: lem-fixedModulus
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
As in the proof of Lemma \ref{lem-imRhoDim1}, let ${\mathcal Y}_p \subset {\mathcal Y}$ be the fiber of $p_1\circ f: {\mathcal Y} \rightarrow {{\mathbb P}}^n$ over $p$. Since ${\mathcal Y}$ is $GL(n+1)$-invariant, the associated line map $\lambda: {\mathcal Y}_p \dashrightarrow {{\mathbb G}}(1,n)$ maps onto the locus of lines through $p$. Let ${\mathcal Y}_{p,\ell}$ be the fiber of $\lambda$ over $[\ell]\in {{\mathbb G}}(1,n)$, where $\ell:=\ell(p,b)$. It is enough to show that ${\mathcal Y}_{p,\ell}$ has 0-dimensional image under $\rho$. We can factor the restriction map $\rho_\ell: {\mathcal Y}_{p,\ell} \dashrightarrow \overline{U}_{0,d}^{\mathop{\mathrm{Sym}}\nolimits}$ as 
    \begin{center}
        \begin{tikzcd} 
            &{\mathcal Y}_{p,\ell} \arrow[rr, dashed, "\rho_\ell"] \arrow[dr, "\rho_1"] & &\overline{U}_{0,d}^{\mathop{\mathrm{Sym}}\nolimits}\\
            & &H^0(\ell,{\mathcal O}_\ell(d)) \arrow[ur, dashed, "\rho_2"]
        \end{tikzcd}.
    \end{center}

    The case $n \geq 3$ follows directly from an argument of Voisin \cite[Lemma 3]{voisinCorrection}, which we summarize here for the reader's convenience. We have a distribution $\mathcal{I} \subset T_{{\mathcal Y}}^{\operatorname{vert}}$ on ${\mathcal Y}$, whose fiber over a general point $(p,b)$ of ${\mathcal Y}$ is precisely $H^0({\mathcal O}_{{{\mathbb P}}^n}(d) \otimes I_{\ell})$. We can understand the Lie bracket map $\psi: \bigwedge^2 \mathcal{I} \to T_{{\mathcal Y}}^{\operatorname{vert}}/\mathcal{I}$ at the point $(p,b)$ explicitly in coordinates, in terms of the differential of the associated line map, which we denote by $\phi: T_{{\mathcal Y}}^{\operatorname{vert}}\vert_{(p,b)} \to T_{\ell} \,{{\mathbb G}}(1,n)_p$. Here ${{\mathbb G}}(1,n)_p$ is the space of lines in ${{\mathbb P}}^n$ passing through $p$, and $ T_{\ell} \,{{\mathbb G}}(1,n)_p \simeq H^0(\ell, N_{\ell / {{\mathbb P}}^n}(-p))$. A local calculation shows that $\phi$ vanishes on $\mathcal{I}^2$, so the map $\psi$ at $(p,b)$ descends to a map
    \[ \psi: \bigwedge^2(H^0({\mathcal O}_{\ell}(d)(-p)) \otimes K^{*}) \to H^0({\mathcal O}_{\ell}(d)(-p)) , \]
    where $K = H^0(\ell, N_{\ell / {{\mathbb P}}^n}(-p))$ and the map is given by $\psi(A \wedge B) = A\cdot\phi(B) - B\cdot\phi(A)$, where $\cdot$ comes from the natural contraction pairing of $K^*$ with $K$. Using \cite[Lemma 4]{voisinCorrection}, it follows that if $\phi$ is nontrivial on $\mathcal I$, the image of $\psi$ must have codimension at most 1 in $H^0({\mathcal O}_{\ell}(d)(-p))$. This contradicts our choice of ${\mathcal Y}$ being codimension $n-1\geq 2$ in ${\mathcal X}$, so it follows that $\phi$ must be trivial on $\mathcal I$. As in \cite{voisinCorrection}, it follows that the vertical tangent space $T_{\rho_1}$ of the map $\rho_1$ contains $H^0({\mathcal O}_{{{\mathbb P}}^n}(d)\otimes I_\ell)$. By the $GL(n+1)$-invariance of ${\mathcal Y}$, the image of $\rho_1$ is closed under the $GL(2)$-actions that fix $p$. The tangent directions corresponding to these actions, which span a space of dimension 3, are contained in the vertical tangent space $T_{\rho_2}$ of $\rho_2$. So, we have the following bound on the dimension of the image of $\rho_\ell$.
    \begin{align*}
        \dim \text{Im }\rho_\ell 
        \leq& \dim {\mathcal Y}_{p,\ell}-h^0({\mathcal O}_{{{\mathbb P}}^n}(d)\otimes I_\ell)-3\\
        =& (\dim {\mathcal Y}_{p}-(n-1))-h^0({\mathcal O}_{{{\mathbb P}}^n}(d)\otimes I_\ell)-3\\
        =& \dim \iota_b^*T_{\mathcal Y}^{\operatorname{vert}}(-\log {\mathcal D})\vert_p -(n-1)-h^0({\mathcal O}_{{{\mathbb P}}^n}(d)\otimes I_\ell)-3\\
        =&(\dim f_b^*T_{\mathcal X}^{\operatorname{vert}}(-\log {\mathcal D})\vert_p-\dim N_{Y_b/{{\mathbb P}}^n}(\log D_b)\vert_p)\\
    &\quad -(n-1)-h^0({\mathcal O}_{{{\mathbb P}}^n}(d)\otimes I_\ell)-3\\
        =&\dim f_b^*T_{\mathcal X}^{\operatorname{vert}}(-\log D)\vert_p-h^0({\mathcal O}_{{{\mathbb P}}^n}(d)\otimes I_\ell)\\
    &\quad -\dim N_{Y_b/{{\mathbb P}}^n}(\log D_b)\vert_p-(n+2)\\
        =&(d+1)-(n-1)-(n+2)\\
        =&d-2n=0.
    \end{align*}
    
    The other case is $n=2$. We have shown in Lemma \ref{lem-imRhoDim1} that $\rho$ has an image of dimension at most one. If the image is 0-dimensional, we are done, so suppose not. We will show that the image of ${\mathcal Y}_p$ in $\overline{U}_{0,4}^{\mathop{\mathrm{Sym}}\nolimits}$ is 0-dimensional. The lifiting ${\mathcal Y} \to B \times V$ restricts to a lifting ${\mathcal Y}_p \to B \times {{\mathbb G}}(1,2)_p$, where ${{\mathbb G}}(1,2)_p$ is the space of lines through $p$. Let $Z$ be the preimage of $\rho({\mathcal Y}_p)$ in $B \times {{\mathbb G}}(1,2)_p$. We see that $Z$ has codimension 1 in $B \times {{\mathbb G}}(1,2)_p$, so that $Z$ maps generically finitely onto ${\mathcal X}_p$, giving an isomorphism of tangent spaces at a general point. The relative tangent space of $Z \to \overline{U}_{0,4}^{\mathop{\mathrm{Sym}}\nolimits}$ is $H^0({{\mathbb P}}^2,I_{\ell}(4)) + M_1|_p\cdot \operatorname{Jac}(F) + F$, coming from the polynomials with fixed restriction to the line together with the automorphisms of ${{\mathbb P}}^2$ fixing $p$ that move the line. By Lemma \ref{lem-P2jumping}, this is the same as $T_{{\mathcal Y}}^{\operatorname{vert}}(-\log {\mathcal D})|_{(p,b)}$, so it follows that ${\mathcal Y}$ must be a fiber of the map to $\overline{U}_{0,4}^{\mathop{\mathrm{Sym}}\nolimits}$, as required.

title: Proof
body_md: This is simply piecing everything together. If for a general hypersurface $D$ we can find a curve violating (\ref{eqn-logah3}) or (\ref{eqn-logah2}), then we can spread the curve out into a universal family as in Proposition \ref{prop-mainSetupProp}. We wish to understand the log normal sheaf. Using Proposition \ref{prop-mainLazarsfeldProp}, we see that it admits a surjection from some copies of pullbacks of $M_1$. By Proposition \ref{prop-m1equals2}, we see that the rank $m_1$ of the image of the first $M_1$ must be 1. By Lemma \ref{lem-2.10}, it follows that we can lift the curve $C$ to $V$. By Lemma \ref{lem-fixedModulus}, it follows that the lifting of $C$ to $V$ must lie in a fiber of $\theta: V \dashrightarrow \overline{U}_{0,d}^{\mathop{\mathrm{Sym}}\nolimits}$ or the undefined locus of $\theta$. The result follows.

label: LANGLOGAH2LEMFIXMODULI
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $C$ meets the dual curve of $D$, there is at least one line $L\in C$ that fails to meet $D$ transversely. Clearly, such $L$ cannot meet $D$ at a point with multiplicity $2$; otherwise, the image of $C$ will meet the boundary point of $\overline{M}_{0,4}^{\mathop{\mathrm{Sym}}\nolimits}$. So for $D$ general, such $L$ can only be a flex line of $D$. It is also clear that two such distinct curves $C_1$ and $C_2$ can only meet at these flex lines.

The map $\gamma: {{\mathbb G}}(1,2)\dashrightarrow M_{0,4}^{\mathop{\mathrm{Sym}}\nolimits}$ is smooth at a line $L\in {{\mathbb G}}(1,2)$ meeting $D$ transversely if and only if we have a surjection
$$
\begin{tikzcd}
H^0(N_{L/{{\mathbb P}}^2}) \ar[two heads]{r} & H^1(T_L(-\log D)) 
\end{tikzcd}
$$
induced by the exact sequence
$$
\begin{tikzcd}
0 \ar{r} & T_L(-\log D) \ar{r} & T_{{{\mathbb P}}^2}(-\log D) \Big|_L \ar{r} & N_{L/{{\mathbb P}}^2}(\log D) = N_{L/ {{\mathbb P}}^2} \ar{r} & 0.
\end{tikzcd}
$$
This happens if and only if $H^1(L, T_{{{\mathbb P}}^2}(-\log D)) = 0$, or equivalently,
$$
T_{{{\mathbb P}}^2}(-\log D)\Big|_L = {\mathcal O}_L(-1) \oplus {\mathcal O}_L.
$$

By Lemma \ref{lem-Ominus2splitting} there are only finitely many such lines $L$. In conclusion, $\gamma$ is smooth outside of a finite set of points plus the dual curve of $D$. Therefore, for $j$ general, $C$ is smooth outside of the $24$ flex lines. Let us figure out the type of singularity of $C$ at a flex line $L$.

For simplicity, suppose that $C$ passes through the flex line $L = \{y = 0\}$ of $D$, where $(x,y)$ are the affine coordinates of ${{\mathbb P}}^2$. In these coordinates, $D$ is given by the affine equation
$$
y g(x,y) + x^3 + c x^4 = 0,
$$
and we can scale so that $g(0,0) = 1$.
Let $(s,t)$ be local coordinates of ${{\mathbb G}}(1,2)$ at $L$, so that a deformation of $L$ in ${{\mathbb G}}(1,2)$ is given by
$$
y = sx + t .
$$
Then $y = sx + t$ meets $D$ at the points
$$
x^3 + sx + t + cx^4 + (sx + t)(g(x, sx + t) - 1) = 0 .
$$
The above equation has four roots $r_i = r_i(s,t)$ for $i=1,2,3,4$, where $r_4 \in {{\mathbb C}}[[s,t]]$ and $r_1, r_2, r_3$ are algebraic functions in $s$ and $t$, defined in some finite extension of ${{\mathbb C}}[[s,t]]$. They satisfy
$$
r_1(0,0) = r_2(0,0) = r_3(0,0) = 0 \text{ and } r_4(0,0) = -\frac{1}c.
$$
The limit of the cross ratio of these four points is
$$
\lambda = \lim_{(s,t)\to (0,0)} \frac{(r_1 - r_2)(r_3 - r_4)}{(r_1 - r_3)(r_2 - r_4)} = \lim_{(s,t)\to (0,0)} \frac{r_1 - r_2}{r_1 - r_3}
$$
Hence $j = j(\lambda)$.

Given the $j$-invariant $j$, there exists a pair $(a, b)$ such that if $r_1,r_2,r_3$ are the three roots of the equation
$$
x^3 + a x + b = 0,
$$
then
$$
j = j\left(\frac{r_1 - r_2}{r_1 - r_3}\right).
$$
The ratio $a^3/b^2$ uniquely characterizes the pairs $(a,b)$ with this property, so we may regard $(a,b)$ as a point in the corresponding weighted projective line ${{\mathbb P}}(2,3)$.

When $a = 0$ and $b\ne 0$, $j = j(-e^{2\pi i/3})$. When $a \ne 0$ and $b = 0$, $j = j(2)$. Suppose that $j\ne j(2), j(-e^{2\pi i/3})$. Then the corresponding $(a,b)$ satisfies $ab \ne 0$.

For some fixed local branch $C$ of a component of a fiber of $\gamma$, let
$$
\left\{
\begin{aligned}
s &= a u^m\\
t &= b u^n + O(u^{n+1})
\end{aligned}\right.
$$
be the local normalization of $C$ at $(0,0)$. Let us consider the roots of
$$
x^3 + (a u^m x + b u^n  + O(u^{n+1})) g(x, a u^m x + b u^n + O(u^{n+1})) + c x^4 = 0.
$$

If $3m > 2n$, then
$$ \lim_{u\to 0} \frac{r_1 - r_2}{r_1 - r_3} = -e^{2\pi i/3} $$
after some permuation of $r_1, r_2, r_3$. This is impossible because we assume that $j\ne j(-e^{2\pi i/3})$.

Similarly, if $3m < 2n$, then
$$ \lim_{u\to 0} \frac{r_1 - r_2}{r_1 - r_3} = 2 $$
after some permuation of $r_1, r_2, r_3$. This is impossible because we assume that $j\ne j(2)$.

So we necessarily have $3m = 2n$. Let us rewrite the normalization as
$$
\left\{
\begin{aligned}
s &= a u^{2l}\\
t &= b u^{3l} (1 + v)
\end{aligned}\right.
$$
where $v = O(u)$ is a function of $u$. Let us consider the roots of
$$
x^3 + (a u^{2l} x + b u^{3l}(1+v)) g(x, a u^{2l} x + b u^{3l} (1+v)) + c x^4 = 0
$$
in ${{\mathbb C}}[[u, v]]$. Clearly, all $r_1, r_2, r_3, r_4$ are functions in $u^l$ and $v$. Furthermore,
$$
\left\{
\begin{aligned}
r_1 &= u^l (c_1 + d_1v + O(u^l, v^2))\\
r_2 &= u^l (c_2 + d_2v + O(u^l, v^2))\\
r_3 &= u^l (c_3 + d_3v + O(u^l, v^2))\\
r_4 &= -\frac{1}c + O(u^{2l}, u^{3l}(1+v))
\end{aligned}\right.
$$
where $c_1, c_2, c_3$ are three roots of $x^3 + ax + b = 0$ and $d_1, d_2, d_3$ are constants satisfying the equations
$$
\left\{
\begin{aligned}
d_1 + d_2 + d_3 &= 0\\
c_1d_1 + c_2 d_2 + c_3 d_3 &= 0\\
c_3 d_1d_2 + c_1 d_2d_3 + c_2 d_3d_1 &= b
\end{aligned}\right.
$$
Since $r_1,r_2, r_3, r_4$ have constant $j$-invariant,
$$
\frac{(r_1 - r_2)(r_3 - r_4)}{(r_1 - r_3)(r_2 - r_4)} \equiv \frac{c_1 - c_2}{c_1 - c_3}
$$
The above equation, viewed as an equation in ${{\mathbb C}}[[u,v]]$, will have non-vanishing coefficient of $v$ provided that
\begin{equation}\label{LANGLOGAH2E001}
\det \begin{bmatrix}
c_1 - c_2 & d_1 - d_2\\
c_1 - c_3 & d_1 - d_3
\end{bmatrix} \ne 0
\end{equation}
which holds provided that $j\ne j(-e^{2\pi i/3})$. Therefore, we may write
$$
v = v(u^l)
$$
for a function $v(w)\in {{\mathbb C}}[[w]]$ satisfying $v(0) = 0$. So the normalization of $C$ is
$$
\left\{
\begin{aligned}
s &= a u^{2l}\\
t &= b u^{3l} (1 + v(u^l))
\end{aligned}\right.
$$
Since the normalization of $C$ is birational onto its image, we must have $l=1$. In conclusion, the normalization of $C$ is given by
\begin{equation}\label{LANGLOGAH2E000}
\left\{
\begin{aligned}
s &= a u^2\\
t &= b u^3(1 + v(u))
\end{aligned}\right.
\end{equation}
for some $v(u) \in {{\mathbb C}}[[u]]$ satisfying $v(0) = 0$. 
That is, when $ab \ne 0$, $C$ has a cusp at $L$.
It follows from the description above that $v(u)$ is uniquely determined by $(a,b)$.

Furthermore, when $b\to 0$, i.e., $j\to j(2)$, the flat limit of $C$ is simply the image of
$(s,t) = (au^2, 0)$, i.e., locally a nonreduced curve supported on a smooth curve with multiplicity $2$. This is due to the fact that \eqref{LANGLOGAH2E001} still holds for $j=j(2)$.

Let us now prove that $C$ passes through all $24$ flex lines and $\deg C = 12$ for $j$ general.
To be more precise, we can extend $\gamma$ to a rational map
$$
\begin{tikzcd}
{{\mathbb G}}(1,2)\times |{\mathcal O}_{{{\mathbb P}}^2}(4)| \ar[dashed]{r}{\gamma} & M_{0,4}^{\mathop{\mathrm{Sym}}\nolimits} \times |{\mathcal O}_{{{\mathbb P}}^2}(4)|
\end{tikzcd}
$$
in an obvious way. We claim that the closure $\overline{\gamma^{-1}(j, D)}$ of $\gamma^{-1}(j, D)$ for $(j,D)$ general is an integral curve $C$ of degree $12$ passing through all $24$ flex lines to $D$. Note that $\overline{\theta^{-1}(j, D)}$, a priori, is not necessarily irreducible.

Let $F$ be the set of $24$ flex lines to $D$.
Let $C_1$ be an irreducible component of $\overline{\gamma^{-1}(j_1, D)}$ for $(j_1,D)$ general. Suppose that $C_1$ passes through a subset $F_1$ of $F$. 
Due to the uniqueness of $v(u)$ in \eqref{LANGLOGAH2E000}, $C_1$ has only one local branch at each line $L\in F_1$.

By \cite{Har79}, the monodromy group on the $24$ flex lines of $D$ is the full symmetric group as $D$ varies. So there is a component $C_1^\sigma$ of $\overline{\gamma^{-1}(j_1, D)}$ passing through $\sigma(F_1)$ for every permutation $\sigma$ of $F$.  

Let $C_2$ be an irreducible component of $\overline{\gamma^{-1}(j_2, D)}$ for $(j_2,D)$ general and $j_2\ne j_1$. Suppose that $C_2$ passes through a subset $F_2$ of $F$. Then $C_1$ and $C_2$ meet only at $L\in F_1\cap F_2$ and $(C_1.C_2)_L = 6$ by \eqref{LANGLOGAH2E000}. Therefore,
$$
C_1 . C_2 = 6 |F_1\cap F_2|
$$
For the same reason, we have
$$
C_1^{\sigma} . C_2 = 6 |\sigma(F_1)\cap F_2|.
$$
Since $\deg C_1 = \deg C_1^{\sigma}$, we conclude that
$$
|F_1\cap F_2| = |\sigma(F_1)\cap F_2|.
$$
This holds for every permutation $\sigma$ on $F$. So we necessarily have $F_1 = F$ or $F_2 = F$.
And since $j_1$ and $j_2$ are general, this implies that
$$
F_1 = F_2 = F \text{ and } \deg C_1 = \deg C_2 = 12.
$$
That is, every component of $\overline{\gamma^{-1}(j, D)}$ is an integral curve of degree $12$ with cusps at $L\in F$ for $(j, D)$ general.

Also $\overline{\gamma^{-1}(j, D)}$ cannot have more than one irreducible component. Otherwise, if $C$ and $C'$ are two distinct irreducible components of $\overline{\gamma^{-1}(j, D)}$, both curves are locally given by \eqref{LANGLOGAH2E000} at each flex line $L\in F$ with the same $a$ and $b$. Hence
$(C.C')_L > 6$
and it follows that $C.C' > 144$, which contradicts the fact that $\deg C = \deg C' = 12$.

This proves that for $(j,D)$ general, $\overline{\gamma^{-1}(j, D)}$ is an integral curve of degree $12$ with cusps at the $24$ flex lines to $D$ and smooth elsewhere. Next, let us prove that this is also true for all $j \ne j(2), j(-e^{2\pi i/3})$ and $D$ general.

Let $\Gamma = \overline{\gamma^{-1}(j, D)}$ for some $j \ne j(2), j(-e^{2\pi i/3})$ and $D$ general, where we consider $\gamma^{-1}(j, D)$ as the scheme-theoretical preimage of $(j,D)$. Since $\Gamma$ is the flat limit of $C = \overline{\gamma^{-1}(j, D)}$ for $(j, D)$ general, $\Gamma$ has degree $12$ and
$(\Gamma . C)_L = 6$ for all flex lines $L\in F$. Every irreducible component of $\Gamma$ has a cusp at $L$ if it passes through $L\in F$. So for every $L\in F$, there exists a unique irreducible component of $\Gamma$ passing through $L$. Therefore, $\Gamma$ must be reduced and irreducible; otherwise, two components $G_1$ and $G_2$ of $\Gamma$ must be disjoint, which is impossible. 

This proves that $\overline{\gamma^{-1}(j, D)}$ is an integral curve of degree $12$ with cusps at the $24$ flex lines to $D$ for all
$j \ne j(2), j(-e^{2\pi i/3})$
and $D$ general.

Finally, let us deal with the cases $j = j(2), j(-e^{2\pi i/3})$. Again, we let $\Gamma = \overline{\gamma^{-1}(j, D)}$. We still have $\deg \Gamma = 12$ and $(\Gamma . C)_L = 6$ for all $L\in F$.

If $j=j(2)$, then $b=0$. Since the flat limit of \eqref{LANGLOGAH2E000} as $b\to 0$ exists, $\Gamma$ is nonreduced with multiplicty $2$ at each $L\in F$. So again, for every $L\in F$, there exists a unique irreducible component of $\Gamma$ passing through $L$. Therefore, $\Gamma$ has a unique irreducible component and hence $\Gamma = 2G$ for an integral curve $G$ of degree $6$.

If $j=j(-e^{2\pi i/3})$, then $a=0$. By \eqref{LANGLOGAH2E000}, $\Gamma$ either is nonreduced with multiplicty $3$ or has a singularity of multiplicity $3$ at each $L\in F$. So again, for every $L\in F$, there exists a unique irreducible component of $\Gamma$ passing through $L$. Therefore, $\Gamma$ has a unique irreducible component; either $\Gamma$ is reduced and irreducible or $\Gamma = 3G$ for an integral curve $G$ of degree $4$. However, in this case, the former is impossible by comparing the arithmetic genus of $\Gamma$ and the $\delta$-invariants of $\Gamma$ at $L\in F$: $p_a(\Gamma) = 55 < 3\cdot 24$.

label: prop-fibersofphiclasses
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop-fibersofphiclasses}
Let $V\subset {{\mathbb P}}^2\times {{\mathbb G}}(1,2)$ be the universal family of lines in ${{\mathbb P}}^2$.
Given a smooth quartic curve $D\subset {{\mathbb P}}^2$, 
let $C$ be an integral curve in $V$ such that the rational map $\theta: V\dashrightarrow \overline{U}_{0,4}^{\mathop{\mathrm{Sym}}\nolimits}$ sending $(p,L)$ to $(p, L\cap D)$ is constant at general points of $C$.
Then $C$ has class $(18,12)$, $(18, 6)$, $(18, 4)$, $(36,12)$ or $(54,12)$ in $V \subset {{\mathbb P}}^2 \times {{\mathbb P}}^2$ for $D$ general.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemma \ref{LANGLOGAH2LEMFIXMODULI}, $\deg \eta(C) = 12, 6$ or $4$, where $\eta: V\to {{\mathbb G}}(1,2)$ is the projection $V\to {{\mathbb G}}(1,2)$. Let $G = \eta(C)$, $S = \eta^{-1}(G)$ and $\nu: \widehat{S} \to V$ be the normalization of $S$. Obviously, $\widehat{S}$ is a ${{\mathbb P}}^1$-bundle over the normalization $\widehat{G}$ of $G$.

Let $\widehat{D} = \nu^* \pi^* D$, where $\pi$ is the projection $V\to {{\mathbb P}}^2$. Clearly, $\widehat{D}$ is a multisection of $\widehat{S}/\widehat{G}$ of degree $4$. The map $\widehat{D}\to \widehat{G}$ is unramified outside of the $24$ flex lines to $D$. Over a flex line $L\in G$, $\widehat{D}$ meets the fiber $\widehat{S}_{_L}$ at two points with multiplicities $1$ and $3$, respectively. Let $p_{_L}$ be the point on $\widehat{S}_{_L}$ where $\widehat{D}$ and $\widehat{S}_{_L}$ intersect with multiplicity $3$. By \eqref{LANGLOGAH2E000}, $\widehat{D}$ has an ordinary triple point at $p_{_L}$. That is, $\widehat{D}$ is locally a union of three sections at $p_{_L}$ that meet each other transversely.

Let $\widehat{C} = \nu^{-1}(C)$ be the proper transform of $C$. Suppose that $\widehat{C}$ is a multisection of $\widehat{S}/\widehat{G}$ of degree $\delta$. 
By our hypothesis, the multisection $\widehat{C}\cup \widehat{D}$ has local constant moduli on the fibers of $\widehat{S}/\widehat{G}$. By our previous argument, over every a flex line $L\in G$, $\widehat{C}\cup \widehat{D}$ is locally a union of $\delta + 3$ sections at $p_{_L}$ that meet each other transversely; otherwise, $\theta(C)$ will meet a boundary component of $\overline{U}_{0,4}^{\mathop{\mathrm{Sym}}\nolimits}$.
Therefore,
$$
(\widehat{C} . \widehat{D})_{p_{_L}} = 3\delta.
$$
Thus, we have
$$
\widehat{C} . \widehat{D} = 3\delta \cdot 24 = 72\delta
$$
and hence
$$
\pi_* C . D = 72\delta.
$$
This implies that $\deg \pi_* C = 18\delta$. In addition, we have $\delta \le 3$. Indeed, $\delta = 1$ if $\deg G = 12$, $\delta = 1$ or $2$ if $\deg G = 6$, and $\delta = 1$ or $3$ if $\deg G = 4$.
head: environment

title: Proposition
body_md: Let $G_4 = \eta^* \eta_* \pi^*T_{{{\mathbb P}}^2}(-\log D)$. Then $G_4$ has first chern class $(0,-7)$ on $V$. Hence, so does $T_\theta$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
First observe that $T_\theta$ and $G_4$ are identical subsheaves of $T_V$ outside of the non-defined locus of $\theta$ and the locus of lines with $T_{{{\mathbb P}}^2}(-\log D)|_\ell = {\mathcal O}(1) \oplus {\mathcal O}(-2)$. By Lemma \ref{lem-Ominus2splitting}, this will be a codimension 2 locus in $V$, so their first chern classes will be the same. Similarly, $R^1 \eta_* \pi^* T_{{{\mathbb P}}^2}(-\log D)$ will be 0 outside of a codimension 2 subset, so it won't affect the calculation of $c_1$. 

Using Grothendieck-Riemann-Roch, we see that $\mathop{\mathrm{ch}}\nolimits(\eta_* \pi^* T_{{{\mathbb P}}^2}(-\log D) ) = \eta_*(\mathop{\mathrm{ch}}\nolimits(\pi^* T_{{{\mathbb P}}^2}(-\log D) \mathop{\mathrm{td}}\nolimits T_{\eta}) .$

Since $T_{\eta} = (-1,2)$, we have $\mathop{\mathrm{td}}\nolimits(T_{\eta}) = 1- \frac{1}{2}H_2+H_1+\frac{1}{12}(-H_2+2H_1)^2$. Using the defining sequence 
\[ 0 \to T_{{{\mathbb P}}^2}(-\log D) \to T_{{{\mathbb P}}^2} \to {\mathcal O}_D(D) \to 0 \]
with the Euler sequence, we see that $\mathop{\mathrm{ch}}\nolimits(T_{{{\mathbb P}}^2}(-\log D)) = 2 - H_1 -\frac{13}{2}H_1^2$.
Combining, we compute $\eta_* ((2-H_1-\frac{13}{2})(1- \frac{1}{2}H_2+H_1+\frac{1}{12}(-H_2+2H_1)^2) = 1-7H + \text{higher terms}$. The result follows.

label: cor-finalFibersCor
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor-finalFibersCor}
Let $C$ be a curve in $V$ in a fiber of the map $\theta$, and suppose that $\pi(C)$ is not a line. Then $\pi(C)$ has degree 18 and $2g(C)-2+i(C,D) \geq 84$. In particular, $2g-2+i \geq \frac{1}{2} \deg C$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: This is a simple chern class calculation. Since $C$ is tangent to $T_\theta$, it follows that $T_C(-\log D \cap C)$ maps to $T_{\theta}$, which implies that its degree is at most the degree of $T_{\theta}|_C$. The result follows from the fact that the class of $C$ is $(18,12)$, $(18, 6)$, or $(18,4)$ by Lemma \ref{LANGLOGAH2LEMFIXMODULI}.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: We have already completed almost all the necessary arguments. For $n=2$, this follows directly from Theorem \ref{thm-associatedLine} and Corollary \ref{cor-finalFibersCor}. For $n>2$, by Theorem \ref{thm-associatedLine}, we know that the only possible counterexamples to (\ref{eqn-logah3}) lie in the fibers and undefined locus of $\theta$, that is, they form a bounded family of curves, which we call $M$. We can stratify $M$ by both the geometric genus and the intersection type with $D$, so it remains to show that no dominant stratum of curves of $M$ can violate algebraic hyperbolicity. Thus, the result follows from Proposition \ref{prop-algGGLfordominantFamiliesOfCurves}.

label: prop-sharpconics
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop-sharpconics}
Let $D$ be a general quartic plane curve in ${{\mathbb P}}^2$. Then there exists a conic in ${{\mathbb P}}^2$ meeting $C$ set-theoretically at three points. Hence, for $S$ equal to the union of the flex and bitangent lines, the inequality in Theorem \ref{thm-varmain} is sharp.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We first compute the dimension of the universal family of such pairs. Let $W$ be the variety of pairs $(C,D)$ where $C$ is a smooth conic and $D$ is a quartic plane curve such that $C$ meets $D$ to order 6 at one point and to order 1 at two other points. We wish to compute the dimension of $W$. There is a natural map $\pi_1$ from $W$ to the space ${{\mathbb P}} H^0({\mathcal O}_{{{\mathbb P}}^2}(2))$ of conics, surjective over the locus of smooth conics. We wish to compute the dimension of a fiber of $\pi_1$. Let $C$ be a smooth conic. Then the map $H^0({{\mathbb P}}^2,{\mathcal O}_{{{\mathbb P}}^2}(4)) \to H^0({\mathcal O}_C(4))$ is surjective, so the dimension of a general fiber of $\pi_1$ has dimension $\dim H^0(\mathcal{I}_{C}(4)) + \dim C \times {\mathfrak S}^2 C = 9$. Thus, the dimension of $W$ is 14, the same as the dimension of the space of quartic plane curves. Observe that $W$ will contain pairs $(C,D)$ with $D$ smooth. To see this, observe that the space of possible $D$ meeting $C$ to order at least 6 at a given point $p$ form a linear system. By Bertini, a general $D$ in the linear system will be smooth away from the base locus $p$. However, we see that the reducible conic $C \cup C_1$ will be in the linear system for some conic $C_1$ not containing $p$, so the general element of the linear system will be smooth at $p$ as well. 

We now claim that the map $\pi_2$ from $W$ to the space of quartic plane curves is generically finite. To see this, note that given a fixed $(C,D)$ in $W$ with $D$ smooth, the deformations of $C$ that still meet $D$ to order 6 at one point will be parameterized by $H^0(N_{C/{{\mathbb P}}^2}(\log D))$. A simple degree calculation shows that the degree of $N_{C/{{\mathbb P}}^2}(\log D)$ is $-1$, and since $C$ and $D$ are both smooth, we see that the normal bundle will be a vector bundle. It follows that $H^0(N_{C/{{\mathbb P}}^2}(\log D)) = 0$, which completes the proof.

title: Proof
body_md:
We follow Demailly's argument in the projective case.
Suppose that there is a nonconstant map $\alpha: A \to {{\mathbb P}}^2 \setminus D$ from a semiabelian variety $A$ to ${{\mathbb P}}^2 \setminus D$ whose image does not lie in $S$. Let $[n]:A \to A$ be the map sending $a\to na$ by the group law and let $f:C \hookrightarrow A$ be a curve in $A$ cut out by $\dim A - 1$ generic very ample divisors. 
Clearly, $h_n = \alpha\circ [n]\circ f: C\to {{\mathbb P}}^2\setminus D$ is nonconstant for all $n$. Let $C\hookrightarrow \overline{C}$ be the completion of $C$ to a smooth projective curve and $\overline{h}_n: \overline{C}\to {{\mathbb P}}^2$ be the completion of $h_n$. Since $\overline{h}_n^{-1}(D)\subset \overline{C} \setminus C$,
$$
2g(\overline{C}) - 2 + |\overline{C} \setminus C| \ge 2g(\overline{C}) - 2 + |\overline{h}_n^{-1}(D)|
$$
Since $\overline{h}_n(C)$ does not lie in $S$, we have
$$
2g(\overline{C}) - 2 + |\overline{C} \setminus C| \ge 2g(\overline{C}) - 2 + |\overline{h}_n^{-1}(D)| \ge \frac{1}2 \deg \overline{h}_n^* L
$$
for $L = {\mathcal O}_{{{\mathbb P}}^2}(1)$ by Theorem \ref{thm-varmain}. This is impossible since $\deg \overline{h}_n^* L\to \infty$ as $n\to \infty$.
